name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_SEQUENCING_Q01 - Increasing stability of +1 oxidation state in Group 13

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following Group \(13\) elements in the correct increasing order of the relative stability of their \(+1\) oxidation state:

\(\mathrm{Al},\ \mathrm{Ga},\ \mathrm{In},\ \mathrm{Tl}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In Group \(13\) elements (valence configuration \(ns^2np^1\)), the \(+3\) oxidation state is most stable for lighter members, whereas the \(+1\) oxidation state becomes progressively more stable down the group due to the inert pair effect.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
Moving down Group \(13\) from \(\mathrm{Al}\) to \(\mathrm{Tl}\), intervening \(d\)- and \(f\)-orbitals are filled in the inner core (\(\mathrm{Ga}\) and \(\mathrm{In}\) have \(d^{10}\) cores; \(\mathrm{Tl}\) has a \(4f^{14}5d^{10}\) core). Because \(d\)- and \(f\)-electrons provide poor shielding, the increased effective nuclear charge holds the outer \(ns^2\) electrons tightly, making them reluctant to participate in bonding. Consequently, only the single \(np^1\) electron is readily involved in bonding for heavier elements, stabilising the \(+1\) state in the order \(\mathrm{Al < Ga < In < Tl}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct increasing order of relative stability of the \(+1\) oxidation state is \(\mathrm{Al < Ga < In < Tl}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_SEQUENCING_Q02 - Decreasing order of catenation in Group 14 elements

questiontext.text:
Arrange the Group \(14\) elements in the correct decreasing order of their tendency to show catenation:

\(\mathrm{C},\ \mathrm{Si},\ \mathrm{Ge},\ \mathrm{Sn},\ \mathrm{Pb}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Catenation is the tendency of atoms of an element to link with one another through covalent bonds to form chains and rings. Its strength depends directly on the \(\mathrm{M-M}\) single bond enthalpy.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
Down Group \(14\), atomic size increases and electronegativity decreases, causing the \(\mathrm{M-M}\) bond enthalpy to decrease: \(\mathrm{C-C}\) (\(348\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) \(\gg \mathrm{Si-Si}\) (\(297\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) \(> \mathrm{Ge-Ge}\) (\(260\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) \(\approx \mathrm{Sn-Sn}\) (\(240\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)). Lead (\(\mathrm{Pb}\)) does not show catenation. Thus, the tendency to catenate decreases as \(\mathrm{C \gg Si > Ge \approx Sn > Pb}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct decreasing order of catenation tendency is \(\mathrm{C \gg Si > Ge \approx Sn > Pb}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_SEQUENCING_Q03 - Sequential stages in the borax bead test

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following events in the correct chronological sequence for performing the borax bead test with cobalt(II) oxide (\(\mathrm{CoO}\)):

  1. Formation of a transparent liquid that solidifies into a glassy bead of \(\mathrm{NaBO_2 + B_2O_3}\)
  2. Formation of a blue-coloured \(\mathrm{Co(BO_2)_2}\) bead in the Bunsen burner flame
  3. Loss of water molecules from \(\mathrm{Na_2B_4O_7\cdot 10H_2O}\) and swelling up to form anhydrous \(\mathrm{Na_2B_4O_7}\)
  4. Heating the glassy bead with \(\mathrm{CoO}\) on a loop of platinum wire

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The borax bead test relies on the thermal dehydration of borax to boric anhydride (\(\mathrm{B_2O_3}\)), which then reacts with transition metal oxides at high temperature to form coloured metaborates.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
1. First, hydrated borax (\(\mathrm{Na_2B_4O_7\cdot 10H_2O}\)) is heated on a platinum wire loop; it loses its water of crystallisation and swells up to form anhydrous \(\mathrm{Na_2B_4O_7}\).
2. On further heating, \(\mathrm{Na_2B_4O_7}\) turns into a transparent liquid that solidifies into a glass-like borax bead consisting of sodium metaborate and boric anhydride (\(\mathrm{2NaBO_2 + B_2O_3}\)).
3. Next, this glassy bead is heated with the transition metal oxide \(\mathrm{CoO}\) in a Bunsen burner flame.
4. Finally, \(\mathrm{B_2O_3}\) reacts with \(\mathrm{CoO}\) to form a characteristic blue-coloured cobalt(II) metaborate bead, \(\mathrm{Co(BO_2)_2}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence is: loss of water and swelling to anhydrous \(\mathrm{Na_2B_4O_7}\) \(\rightarrow\) solidification into glassy \(\mathrm{NaBO_2 + B_2O_3}\) bead \(\rightarrow\) heating with \(\mathrm{CoO}\) on a platinum wire loop \(\rightarrow\) formation of the blue \(\mathrm{Co(BO_2)_2}\) bead, corresponding to (iii) \(\rightarrow\) (i) \(\rightarrow\) (iv) \(\rightarrow\) (ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_SEQUENCING_Q04 - Preparation and thermal dehydration of orthoboric acid

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following chemical steps in the correct sequence starting from aqueous borax to the formation of a metal borate:

  1. Heating metaboric acid further to yield boric oxide (\(\mathrm{B_2O_3}\))
  2. Acidifying an aqueous solution of borax with \(\mathrm{HCl}\) to form orthoboric acid (\(\mathrm{H_3BO_3}\))
  3. Reacting boric oxide with a basic metallic oxide to form a metal borate
  4. Heating orthoboric acid above \(370\text{ K}\) to form metaboric acid (\(\mathrm{HBO_2}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Orthoboric acid is prepared by acidifying borax and undergoes stepwise thermal dehydration upon heating to yield metaboric acid and ultimately acidic boric oxide (\(\mathrm{B_2O_3}\)).

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
1. Acidifying an aqueous solution of borax with \(\mathrm{HCl}\) yields orthoboric acid: \(\mathrm{Na_2B_4O_7 + 2HCl + 5H_2O \rightarrow 2NaCl + 4B(OH)_3}\).
2. Heating orthoboric acid above \(370\text{ K}\) dehydrates it to metaboric acid: \(\mathrm{H_3BO_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} HBO_2 + H_2O}\).
3. Further heating of metaboric acid yields boric oxide (boric anhydride): \(2\mathrm{HBO_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} B_2O_3 + H_2O}\).
4. Because \(\mathrm{B_2O_3}\) is an acidic oxide, it reacts with basic metallic oxides to form metal borates.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct logical sequence is: acidification of borax to \(\mathrm{H_3BO_3}\) \(\rightarrow\) heating above \(370\text{ K}\) to \(\mathrm{HBO_2}\) \(\rightarrow\) further heating to \(\mathrm{B_2O_3}\) \(\rightarrow\) reaction with a basic metallic oxide to form a metal borate, corresponding to (ii) \(\rightarrow\) (iv) \(\rightarrow\) (i) \(\rightarrow\) (iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_SEQUENCING_Q05 - Mechanistic steps in hydrolysis of silicon tetrachloride

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following mechanistic stages of the hydrolysis of silicon tetrachloride (\(\mathrm{SiCl_4}\)) in the correct chronological order:

  1. Elimination of the first \(\mathrm{HCl}\) molecule to form \(\mathrm{SiCl_3(OH)}\)
  2. Acceptance of a lone pair of electrons from the oxygen atom of a water molecule into a vacant \(3d\)-orbital of \(\mathrm{Si}\)
  3. Complete conversion into silicic acid, \(\mathrm{Si(OH)_4}\)
  4. Stepwise reaction of \(\mathrm{SiCl_3(OH)}\) with three more \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) molecules accompanied by loss of three \(\mathrm{HCl}\) molecules

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Silicon tetrachloride (\(\mathrm{SiCl_4}\)) undergoes rapid nucleophilic hydrolysis in water because silicon possesses vacant \(3d\)-orbitals capable of accepting a lone pair of electrons from \(\mathrm{H_2O}\).

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
1. Initially, the oxygen atom of a water molecule donates a lone pair of electrons into a vacant \(3d\)-orbital of the central \(\mathrm{Si}\) atom in \(\mathrm{SiCl_4}\).
2. Next, one \(\mathrm{HCl}\) molecule is eliminated, yielding the monosubstituted intermediate \(\mathrm{SiCl_3(OH)}\).
3. Subsequently, \(\mathrm{SiCl_3(OH)}\) reacts stepwise with three more \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) molecules, eliminating three more \(\mathrm{HCl}\) molecules.
4. Finally, all four chlorine atoms are replaced by hydroxyl groups, yielding silicic acid, \(\mathrm{Si(OH)_4}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence is: lone-pair donation from \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) to \(3d\)-orbital of \(\mathrm{Si}\) \(\rightarrow\) elimination of first \(\mathrm{HCl}\) to give \(\mathrm{SiCl_3(OH)}\) \(\rightarrow\) reaction with three more \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) losing three \(\mathrm{HCl}\) \(\rightarrow\) complete conversion into \(\mathrm{Si(OH)_4}\), corresponding to (ii) \(\rightarrow\) (i) \(\rightarrow\) (iv) \(\rightarrow\) (iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_SEQUENCING_Q06 - Industrial synthesis and chain-length control of silicones

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following steps in the correct sequence for the preparation of a chain-length-controlled straight-chain silicone polymer starting from silicon:

  1. Hydrolysis of \((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{SiCl_2}\) to form \((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{Si(OH)_2}\)
  2. Condensation polymerisation of \((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{Si(OH)_2}\) with elimination of water
  3. Reaction of silicon with methyl chloride in the presence of \(\mathrm{Cu}\) catalyst at \(573\text{ K}\) to produce \((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{SiCl_2}\)
  4. Addition of \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{SiCl}\) to block the ends of the polymer chain

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Silicones are organosilicon polymers with \((\mathrm{R_2SiO})\) repeating units, manufactured by reacting silicon with alkyl halides, hydrolysing the resulting chlorosilanes, and performing condensation polymerisation.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
1. First, methyl chloride reacts with silicon in the presence of copper catalyst at \(573\text{ K}\) to form methyl-substituted chlorosilanes, principally dimethyldichlorosilane, \((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{SiCl_2}\).
2. Next, \((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{SiCl_2}\) undergoes hydrolysis with water (eliminating \(2\mathrm{HCl}\)) to yield \((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{Si(OH)_2}\).
3. Then, \((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{Si(OH)_2}\) undergoes condensation polymerisation with elimination of \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) to form straight-chain silicone polymers.
4. To control the chain length, \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{SiCl}\) (which hydrolyses to monofunctional \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{SiOH}\)) is added to block the terminal ends of the growing polymer chain.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence is: \(\mathrm{Si + CH_3Cl}\) at \(573\text{ K}\) \(\rightarrow\) hydrolysis of \((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{SiCl_2}\) \(\rightarrow\) condensation polymerisation \(\rightarrow\) end-blocking with \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{SiCl}\), corresponding to (iii) \(\rightarrow\) (i) \(\rightarrow\) (ii) \(\rightarrow\) (iv).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_SEQUENCING_Q07 - Increasing order of first ionisation enthalpy in Group 13

questiontext.text:
Arrange the Group \(13\) elements in the correct increasing order of their first ionisation enthalpy (\(\Delta_i H_1\)):

\(\mathrm{B},\ \mathrm{Al},\ \mathrm{Ga},\ \mathrm{In},\ \mathrm{Tl}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ionisation enthalpy in Group \(13\) does not decrease smoothly down the group because of discontinuities caused by the poor shielding of intervening \(3d\)-electrons in \(\mathrm{Ga}\) and \(4f\)-electrons in \(\mathrm{Tl}\).

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
From the experimental atomic data for Group \(13\):
- \(\mathrm{In}\): \(558\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
- \(\mathrm{Al}\): \(577\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
- \(\mathrm{Ga}\): \(579\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) (slightly higher than \(\mathrm{Al}\) due to poor shielding by \(10\) \(3d\)-electrons)
- \(\mathrm{Tl}\): \(589\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) (higher than \(\mathrm{In}\) due to poor shielding by \(14\) \(4f\)-electrons and \(10\) \(5d\)-electrons)
- \(\mathrm{B}\): \(801\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) (highest due to its very small atomic size)
Comparing these values gives \(\mathrm{In < Al < Ga < Tl < B}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct increasing order of first ionisation enthalpy is \(\mathrm{In < Al < Ga < Tl < B}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_SEQUENCING_Q08 - Increasing order of C-C bond lengths in carbon allotropes

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following carbon–carbon bonds in the correct increasing order of their bond lengths:

  1. \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond length in diamond
  2. \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond length within a hexagonal layer of graphite
  3. Shorter \(\mathrm{C-C}\) (double) bond distance in Buckminsterfullerene (\(\mathrm{C_{60}}\))
  4. Longer \(\mathrm{C-C}\) (single) bond distance in Buckminsterfullerene (\(\mathrm{C_{60}}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Carbon–carbon bond lengths depend on the hybridisation of carbon and the degree of \(\pi\)-bonding (bond order) in the allotrope.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
Listing the exact experimental bond lengths in the three crystalline allotropes of carbon:
- Shorter \(\mathrm{C-C}\) (double) bond in \(\mathrm{C_{60}}\): \(138.3\text{ pm}\)
- In-layer \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond in graphite: \(141.5\text{ pm}\)
- Longer \(\mathrm{C-C}\) (single) bond in \(\mathrm{C_{60}}\): \(143.5\text{ pm}\)
- Tetrahedral \(\mathrm{C-C}\) single bond in diamond: \(154\text{ pm}\)
Ordering from shortest to longest gives: \(138.3\text{ pm} < 141.5\text{ pm} < 143.5\text{ pm} < 154\text{ pm}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct increasing order of bond lengths is: shorter \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond in \(\mathrm{C_{60}}\) < in-layer \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond in graphite < longer \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond in \(\mathrm{C_{60}}\) < \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond in diamond, corresponding to (iii) < (ii) < (iv) < (i).
